title: State-Building in the Americas and Africa
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: From c. 1200 to c. 1450 the Americas and Africa hosted large, sophisticated, well-organized states that built monumental cities, managed complex economies, and governed millions of people. They were neither primitive nor isolated, and often achieved this without the wheel for transport, large draft animals, or, in some cases, writing.

In 1324, Mansa Musa, ruler of the Mali Empire, passed through Cairo on his pilgrimage to Mecca, distributing and spending so much gold that he flooded the local market and the value of gold reportedly dropped for years afterward. The episode demonstrates the immense wealth of a West African empire.

The Aztecs, more properly called the Mexica, built an empire in the Valley of Mexico. According to tradition they founded their capital Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco around 1325, and in 1428 they formed the Triple Alliance with two neighboring cities and expanded by conquest.

Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, grew into a metropolis of perhaps 200,000 people, larger than almost any city in Europe at the time. Built on an island and laced with canals and causeways, it was the center of the Aztec tribute empire.

Chinampas were artificial 'floating gardens' of fertile mud built up in the shallow waters of Lake Texcoco by the Aztecs. This intensive agricultural system was productive enough to feed the huge urban population of Tenochtitlan.

The Aztec Empire was a tribute empire: rather than tightly governing conquered peoples, the Mexica left local rulers in place but demanded heavy regular tribute in goods, textiles, food, and captives. This made the empire wealthy but loosely held and left conquered groups resentful.

Aztec religion was central to the state and required human sacrifice, which the Mexica believed was necessary to keep the sun moving and the cosmos in balance. War and conquest supplied the captives used in these sacrifices.

The Mississippian culture of North America, centered on the city of Cahokia near present-day St. Louis, flourished from around 1050 to 1350. At its peak Cahokia held tens of thousands of people and was dominated by enormous earthen mounds, one of them larger at its base than the Great Pyramid.

The Ancestral Puebloans of the arid North American Southwest built dramatic multi-story cliff dwellings and the great houses of Chaco Canyon. They are an example of the complex, organized societies that existed across North America.

The Inca built a centralized empire in the Andes Mountains called Tawantinsuyu, expanding rapidly after about 1438 from their capital Cuzco. At its height it stretched roughly 2,500 miles down western South America and governed perhaps ten million people.

The mit'a was the Inca labor system that required subjects to provide rotating labor service such as building roads, farming state lands, serving in the army, or working mines. In exchange the state stored surplus goods and redistributed them in times of need.

The Inca ran a state-controlled command economy rather than a market economy. The government, not merchants, organized production and distribution, storing food and goods in vast warehouses and redistributing them across the empire.

The Inca built an extraordinary road network of tens of thousands of miles of stone roads with rope suspension bridges and waystations. This system allowed messages and armies to move quickly through the difficult Andean mountain terrain.

The khipu (also spelled quipu) was a system of knotted, colored cords the Inca used to record numbers and other information in place of writing. Officials used khipu to track labor obligations, populations, and storehouse contents across the empire.
The Inca state religion centered on the sun god Inti, and the emperor was regarded as the sun's living descendant. This fused religious and political authority in the person of the ruler.

The Aztec and Inca empires solved the problem of governing power in opposite ways: the Aztec state was a loose tribute empire that left local rulers in place, while the Inca state was tightly centralized and extracted compulsory rotating labor through the mit'a.

The trans-Saharan trade carried West African gold north and Saharan salt south across the desert in camel caravans. Gold was mined in West African forests and salt in the Sahara, and states that controlled this trade grew rich by taxing it.

The Mali Empire was founded around 1235 by the ruler Sundiata, whose story survives in a great oral epic. Sitting astride the Niger River and the southern desert trade routes, Mali grew fabulously wealthy from the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt.

Mansa Musa was the most famous ruler of the Mali Empire, reigning in the early 1300s. His spectacular pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 broadcast Mali's wealth across the Islamic world and led European and Arab mapmakers to depict Mali and Mansa Musa on their maps.

Timbuktu, a city in the Mali Empire, became a celebrated center of Islamic learning with universities, libraries, and thousands of manuscripts. It reflected how Islam connected West African elites to the wider Muslim world of scholarship and trade.

Islam spread into West Africa along the trans-Saharan trade routes and was adopted by rulers like Mansa Musa, who built mosques and patronized scholarship. However, Islam was often a religion of rulers, merchants, and city-dwellers, while many ordinary people kept indigenous traditions, producing a blended, uneven conversion.

The Swahili city-states of the East African coast, including Kilwa, Mombasa, and Mogadishu, were independent merchant cities that grew wealthy on Indian Ocean trade. They connected the African interior, which exported gold, ivory, and enslaved people, to the wider Indian Ocean world.

The Swahili language is a Bantu African language enriched with many Arabic loanwords, a linguistic fingerprint of centuries of Indian Ocean trade contact. The Swahili elite converted to Islam and built coral-stone towns, making the coast a textbook example of trade producing cultural and religious blending.

Great Zimbabwe was a powerful southern African state whose capital featured massive dry-stone walls built without mortar. It grew rich by controlling the flow of gold from the interior toward the Swahili coast.

The Christian kingdom of Ethiopia in the northeastern African highlands continued an ancient tradition descended from the earlier kingdom of Aksum. Ruled by the Solomonic dynasty, it remained Christian amid Muslim and traditional-religion neighbors and carved remarkable rock churches at Lalibela during this period.

States in the Americas and Africa consolidated power through different strategies: tribute in goods (Aztec), compulsory labor (Inca mit'a), and taxing long-distance trade (Mali, the Swahili city-states, Great Zimbabwe). Religion was often used to legitimize rulers, such as the sun-descended Inca emperor or the Muslim pilgrim-king Mansa Musa.

The organization of the Aztec and Inca empires shaped how they later fell to the Spanish: the Aztec tribute system left resentful conquered peoples willing to ally against Tenochtitlan, while the centralized Inca state's dependence on its god-emperor made capturing the ruler especially paralyzing.
